They tell the compiler "trust me", and because Dart's null safety is sound, the compiler turns that promise into a runtime check that throws on that exact line if you were wrong. Use them only where you can prove the value is there; everywhere else, let a null check promote the type.

It's an understandable habit. The analyzer sometimes really can't see what you can: Dart's own guide shows a response class where

is never read when it's null, a relationship the type checker can't follow. IDEs offer "add a null check" as a one-click fix. And developers who come from TypeScript or C# carry over the rule that a postfix
changes nothing at runtime, which is exactly what those languages' docs say about their versions of it. In Dart, it does.
Sound null safety is a guarantee, not a lint
In Dart, types are non-nullable by default:

, enforced since Dart 3, the promise is strong: if an expression's static type doesn't permit null, no execution of it can ever produce null. The analyzer errors you see are how Dart keeps that promise before your code runs, and Dart's docs credit the design with fewer bugs, smaller binaries and faster execution.
So when you write something the compiler can't prove, Dart doesn't simply take your word for it. To keep the guarantee sound, it inserts a check that runs every time.
is a cast that's checked at runtime
takes the expression on its left and casts it to the underlying non-nullable type. Dart's guide is direct: the cast must be checked at runtime, and
always throws if the value is null. It doesn't fix the null. It converts a compile-time error into a possible runtime exception, on that line.
